div.head: Ine 68
div.ab: CXII. Gif mon gesiðcundne monnan adrife, fordrife þy botle, næs þære setene.
CXII. Gif mon gesiðcundne mon adrife, fordrife þy botle, næs þære setene.
Be gesiðcundes mannes drafe of lande. Gyf mon gesiðcundne monnan adrife, fordrife ðy botle, næs ðære setene.
Si homo siþcundus fugetur, profugio domus, non erit ipsius sedis.
[Be gesiðcundes mannes drafe of lande.] Gif mon gesiðcundne monnan adrife, fordrife þy botle, næs þære setene.
{CXII} Gif mon gesiðcundne monnan adrife, fordrife þy botle, næs þære setene.
Wenn man einen Mann vom Gefolgsadel abzuziehen zwingt, mag man ihn [zwar] von [dessen] Hofe vertreiben, aber nicht von der [durch ihn] bestellten Flur.
If one forces a man of the retainer nobility to move away, one may [indeed] drive him from [his] dwelling, but not from the land [he has] sown.
If a nobleman is evicted, he may be expelled from his house, but not from the cultivated land.
If a gesith-born man is evicted, he is to be evicted from the dwelling, but certainly not from the cultivated land.
If a nobleman is driven away, let him be driven from his dwelling, but not from his cultivated land.

Im Ggs. zu 63—66 löst hier der Herr das læn (s. d. Gl 3; Gefolgsadel 17 c) auf
In contrast to 63–66, here the lord dissolves the læn (see that word in Gl 3; Gefolgsadel 17 c)
næs, stärker als bloss einfache Verneinung, setzt Folgendes in Ggs. zu Vorigem; vgl. bei Toller: riht, næs idel; agnum, næs þinum; dædum, næs wordum
næs, stronger than a mere simple negative, sets what follows in contrast to what precedes; cf. in Toller: riht, næs idel; agnum, næs þinum; dædum, næs wordum

Vgl. Gl säen 4. Dem um Busszahlung (oder Pachtschuld nach Common law) zu pfändenden Villan verbleibt guagnage (die Ernte); Tait in Engl. hist. rev. 27, 722; Pollock Land laws 140. Vgl. auch H. Meyer in Hoops Reallex. Germ. Altt. I 534. Unter den Bedd. von seten passt hier plantatio, -taria der Glossen: ‘what he had planted’ (Toller). — Wie in 67 æcer steht hier seten in Ggs. zu bott. — ‘Inventar’ versteht Price aus landseten (s. Wb); das aber stellte der Herr bei Ausleihung des Bodens und nahm es mit diesem zurück. — ‘Sitz’ Q, wohl verwechselt mit setl

Cf. Gl säen 4. The villein who is to be distrained for payment of compensation (or, under common law, for rent owed) keeps his guagnage (the crop); Tait in Engl. hist. rev. 27, 722; Pollock Land laws 140. Cf. also H. Meyer in Hoops Reallex. Germ. Altt. I 534. Among the meanings of seten, the glosses’ plantatio, -taria fits here: ‘what he had planted’ (Toller). — As æcer in 67, so here seten stands in contrast to bott. — Price understands ‘stock’ from landseten (see Wb); but this the lord provided when leasing out the land, and took back together with it. — ‘Seat’ Q, probably confused with setl

It is not clear to me what this law means. B. and T. (s.v. seten, p. 866) suggest ‘the ejected tenant was not to be deprived of what he had planted?’ or ‘that he was to be compensated for the cultivation of the land?’ Seten may possibly be used in the sense of landseten, ‘land in occupation,’ i.e. land occupied by tenants (cf. cap. 64 above). Seebohm (Tribal Custom in A.S. Law, p. 432 f.) suggests that seten refers to the gesiðcundman’s own cattle and crops (see also Liebermann’s note ad loc.). Is it possible that fordrifan can here mean ‘to undertake hostilities against’?
